notes.front: What is a one-way trust between two domains?
notes.back: A trust that works in one direction only: users of the trusted domain can reach resources in the trusting domain, not the reverse.
notes.explanation: Microsoft describes it as a unidirectional authentication path; the trusting side cannot use that same trust to reach the trusted side.
notes.example: Like a reading room that honours another library's cards, while its own card holders get nothing at that other library.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “One-way and two-way trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a two-way trust between two domains?
notes.back: A trust in both directions: each domain trusts the other, so authentication requests can pass either way.
notes.explanation: Microsoft notes that whether such a trust is also transitive depends on the type of trust being created.
notes.example: Like two neighbouring gyms that let each other's members train at either site.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “One-way and two-way trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a transitive trust?
notes.back: A trust that can be extended beyond the two domains that formed it, to other domains.
notes.explanation: Transitivity is the property Microsoft uses to decide whether trust reaches past the original pair; a non-transitive trust is used to deny that extension.
notes.example: Like accepting a colleague's vouching for a stranger because you already trust the colleague.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “Transitive and non-transitive trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an intranet?
notes.back: An organisation's own network, often built on internet technology, kept for internal use and shut to outsiders.
notes.explanation: The glossary says such a network is usually private: what marks it out is internal use and being closed to people outside the organisation.
notes.example: Like a staff-only wiki and leave-booking portal that only company devices can reach.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “intranet” (from RFC 4949 via CNSSI 4009-2022)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an extranet?
notes.back: A network an organisation uses to carry application data between itself and its business partners.
notes.explanation: Unlike an intranet, which is closed to outsiders, this network exists for traffic with parties outside the organisation.
notes.example: Like a private link a hospital uses to exchange lab orders and results with an outside pathology laboratory.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “extranet” (from RFC 4949 via CNSSI 4009-2022)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an interconnection security agreement (ISA)?
notes.back: One of the agreement types used to approve and manage the exchange of information between a system and other systems.
notes.explanation: The information exchange control lists it beside other options, such as memoranda of understanding and service level agreements; the organisation selects which to use.
notes.evidence: Approve and manage the exchange of information between the system and other systems using [Selection (one or more): interconnection security agreements; information exchange security agreements; memoranda of understanding or agreement; service level agreements;
notes.example: Like a signed contract two firms agree before their payroll and pension systems start swapping files, saying who protects what.
notes.source: SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CA-3 Information Exchange

notes.front: What is an application programming interface (API)?
notes.back: The interface through which software components, such as microservices, communicate with one another.
notes.explanation: Because so many components interact through them, the guidance says core features such as authentication and access management are needed to support those interactions.
notes.evidence: generally communicate with each other using Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), which requires several core features to support complex interactions between a substantial number of components. These core features include authentication and access management
notes.example: Like a restaurant's order hatch: diners use a fixed set of requests and never see how the kitchen works.
notes.source: SP 800-204, Security Strategies for Microservices-based Application Systems, Abstract

notes.front: What is an API gateway?
notes.back: An architectural framework that gives all clients a single entry point to an application's many microservices.
notes.explanation: A microservices application has many fine-grained endpoints rather than a single server, which is why one entry point for clients makes sense.
notes.evidence: Unlike a monolithic application where the endpoint may be a single server, a microservices-based application consists of multiple fine-grained endpoints. Hence, it makes sense to provide a single entry point for all clients to multiple component microservices of the application.
notes.example: Like a hotel reception desk that passes each guest request to housekeeping, the kitchen or maintenance.
notes.source: SP 800-204, §2.7.1 API Gateway

notes.front: In a one-way forest trust, whose members can use resources: the trusted forest's or the trusting forest's?
notes.back: The trusted forest's members can use resources in the trusting forest.
notes.explanation: The trust operates in one direction only, so members of the trusting forest gain no access to the trusted forest through it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “Forest trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Microsoft notes that every two-way trust is really {{c1::two one-way trusts running in opposite directions}}.
notes.explanation: That is why the routine change of the shared trust password, made every 30 days, happens twice for a two-way trust.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “TDO password changes”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does a non-transitive trust do with the domains beyond its own two?
notes.back: It denies them: the trust cannot be extended past the two domains that formed it.
notes.explanation: Microsoft uses transitivity as the test of whether a trust can reach outside the pair of domains that created it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “Transitive and non-transitive trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can a forest trust be implicitly extended to a third forest?
notes.back: No. A forest trust links exactly two forests; a third forest needs a trust of its own.
notes.explanation: For users in two outer forests to share resources, Microsoft says a two-way transitive trust must be created directly between those two forests.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “Forest trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When a new domain is added to an Active Directory forest, what trust is created with its parent domain?
notes.back: A two-way, transitive trust, created automatically.
notes.explanation: These trust paths flow up the domain tree, so accounts from any domain in the forest can be authenticated by any other domain in it.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “Transitive and non-transitive trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Each information exchange agreement documents the interface characteristics, security and privacy requirements, controls and responsibilities for each system, and the {{c1::impact level}} of the information communicated.
notes.explanation: The control also asks for the agreements to be reviewed and updated at a frequency the organisation defines.
notes.evidence: Document, as part of each exchange agreement, the interface characteristics, security and privacy requirements, controls, and responsibilities for each system, and the impact level of the information communicated; and c. Review and update the agreements
notes.source: SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CA-3 Information Exchange

notes.front: What decides which type of information exchange agreement is chosen?
notes.back: Factors such as the impact level of the information and the relationship between the organisations exchanging it, among others.
notes.explanation: Authorising officials determine the risk of the exchange and the controls needed to mitigate it, so the agreement is matched to that risk.
notes.evidence: Authorizing officials determine the risk associated with system information exchange and the controls needed for appropriate risk mitigation. The types of agreements selected are based on factors such as the impact level of the information being exchanged, the relationship between the organizations exchanging information
notes.source: SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CA-3 Information Exchange, Discussion

notes.front: Do information exchange requirements cover only connections to systems outside the organisation?
notes.back: No. They also cover exchanges between systems within the same organisation.
notes.explanation: The risk comes from connecting to any system that may have different security and privacy requirements and controls, which can bring new or increased threats.
notes.evidence: Organizations consider the risk related to new or increased threats that may be introduced when systems exchange information with other systems that may have different security and privacy requirements and controls. This includes systems within the same organization and systems that are external to the organization.
notes.source: SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CA-3 Information Exchange, Discussion

notes.front: What is the primary function of an API gateway?
notes.back: To route inbound requests to the correct downstream services.
notes.explanation: Beyond routing, it can optionally translate between protocols, and it sometimes composes requests.
notes.evidence: The primary function of the API gateway is to always route inbound requests to the correct down-stream services, optionally perform protocol translation
notes.source: SP 800-204, §2.7.1 API Gateway

notes.front: How should access to microservice APIs that handle sensitive data be authenticated?
notes.back: With authentication tokens that are digitally signed or verified with an authoritative source, not simply with API keys.
notes.explanation: The microservices guidance lists this among its authentication strategies for APIs that can reach sensitive data.
notes.evidence: done simply by using API keys. Access to such APIs should require authentication tokens that have either been digitally signed (e.g., client credentials grant) or is verified with an authoritative source
notes.source: SP 800-204, §4.1 Strategies for Identity and Access Management (MS-SS-1)

notes.front: Why does an API gateway limit the rate of requests reaching a microservice?
notes.back: To keep the service available for all clients.
notes.explanation: The guidance also calls rate limiting throttling, and lists it among the core features a gateway generally implements.
notes.evidence: Rate limiting (throttling): The rate of requests coming into a microservice must be limited to ensured continued availability of service for all clients.
notes.source: SP 800-204, §2.6 Microservices: State of the Practice Core Features

notes.front: Staff in a newly acquired subsidiary's domain must open files on your company's servers. Your own staff need nothing from the subsidiary. Which trust fits best?
notes.choices:
A) A two-way transitive trust between the domains
B) A one-way trust in which your domain trusts the subsidiary's domain
C) A one-way trust in which the subsidiary's domain trusts your domain
D) No trust at all, with shared passwords instead
notes.back: B: A one-way trust in which your domain trusts the subsidiary's domain.
notes.explanation: Members of the trusted side reach resources on the trusting side, so the domain holding the files must be the one that trusts.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because it also opens the subsidiary's resources to your staff, which nobody asked for. C is wrong because it points the wrong way: your staff would reach the subsidiary, not the reverse. D is wrong because shared passwords are not a trust relationship and give no controlled authentication path.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “Forest trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A client's domain will trust an outside consultancy's domain. The client insists that no other domain the consultancy trusts may gain access through this link. What property should the trust have?
notes.choices:
A) Two-way
B) Non-transitive
C) Transitive
D) Forest-wide
notes.back: B: Non-transitive.
notes.explanation: A non-transitive trust stays between the two domains that formed it, which is exactly the limit the client wants.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because direction does not stop the trust spreading to other domains, and a second direction was not asked for. C is wrong because a transitive trust is the kind that extends to other domains. D is wrong because a wider scope is the opposite of the containment required.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, How trust relationships work for forests in Active Directory, “Transitive and non-transitive trusts”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A council launches an online form for residents to book bulky-waste collections. Its server must be reachable from the internet; the payroll system must stay internal. Where does the form's server best go?
notes.choices:
A) On the internal protected network beside payroll
B) On the firewall's DMZ
C) On the council's intranet
D) On an extranet shared with suppliers
notes.back: B: On the firewall's DMZ.
notes.explanation: Public-facing servers commonly sit on the DMZ, and traffic from there to the protected network still has to pass the firewall.
notes.evidence: It is common to put public-facing servers, such as web and email servers, on the DMZ.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because it puts an internet-facing host among internal systems. C is wrong because an intranet is closed to outsiders, yet residents must reach the form. D is wrong because an extranet serves business partners, not the public.
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §3.1 Network Layouts with Firewalls

notes.front: A logistics firm builds a network over which its contracted hauliers exchange delivery data with the firm's dispatch application. What kind of network is it?
notes.choices:
A) An intranet
B) A DMZ
C) The public internet
D) An extranet
notes.back: D: An extranet.
notes.explanation: It carries application data between the organisation and its business partners, the hauliers.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because an intranet is closed to outsiders, and the hauliers are outsiders. B is wrong because a DMZ is a firewall interface for hosts such as public servers, not a partner network. C is wrong because the network was built for named partners, not everyone.
notes.source: NIST CSRC Glossary, “extranet” (from RFC 4949 via CNSSI 4009-2022)
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under a zero trust architecture, a company laptop plugs into the office's wired network. What must happen before it opens a session to the finance application?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more: the office network is trusted
B) Only the user needs to sign in
C) Subject and device are authenticated and authorised as separate steps
D) Access is granted because the laptop is company-owned
notes.back: C: Subject and device are authenticated and authorised as separate steps.
notes.explanation: Zero trust grants no implicit trust for being on the local network or for company ownership, and checks both subject and device before a session.
notes.evidence: Zero trust assumes there is no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location (i.e., local area networks versus the internet) or based on asset ownership (enterprise or personally owned). Authentication and authorization (both subject and device) are discrete functions performed before a session to an enterprise resource is established.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because network location alone earns no trust. B is wrong because the device must be checked too, not only the user. D is wrong because ownership of the asset earns no implicit trust either.
notes.source: SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, Abstract

notes.front: Two public bodies plan to connect their case-management systems to swap records. Before the link goes live, what does the information exchange control call for?
notes.choices:
A) A verbal understanding between the two system administrators
B) Nothing, as long as both systems are already authorised
C) Approve and manage the exchange with an agreement, such as an ISA
D) Encrypting the link, which replaces any agreement
notes.back: C: Approve and manage the exchange with an agreement, such as an ISA.
notes.explanation: The control asks for information exchanges to be approved and managed through a selected type of agreement, of which an ISA is one.
notes.evidence: Approve and manage the exchange of information between the system and other systems using [Selection (one or more): interconnection security agreements; information exchange security agreements; memoranda of understanding or agreement; service level agreements;
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the control applies to the exchange itself, whatever each system's own status. A is wrong because the control names documented agreement types, not informal ones. D is wrong because encryption is a technical safeguard; it does not approve or document the exchange.
notes.source: SP 800-53 Rev. 5, CA-3 Information Exchange

notes.front: A microservice API returns patients' medical histories. A developer protects it with one static API key built into the mobile app. What does the microservices guidance recommend instead?
notes.choices:
A) A longer API key
B) Removing authentication and relying on the firewall
C) Authentication tokens that are digitally signed or verified with an authoritative source
D) Moving the API key into the app's settings file
notes.back: C: Authentication tokens that are digitally signed or verified with an authoritative source.
notes.explanation: The guidance says APIs that can reach sensitive data should not be authenticated simply by API keys.
notes.evidence: done simply by using API keys. Access to such APIs should require authentication tokens that have either been digitally signed (e.g., client credentials grant) or is verified with an authoritative source
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because a longer key is still only an API key. B is wrong because it drops authentication altogether. D is wrong because moving the key does not change the fact that it is a bare API key.
notes.source: SP 800-204, §4.1 Strategies for Identity and Access Management (MS-SS-1)

notes.front: A shopping app's clients call eight different microservice endpoints directly. Which change do the microservices security strategies recommend?
notes.choices:
A) Give each client a list of every service address
B) Point clients at the single gateway address instead of the services
C) Merge all eight services back into one server
D) Let each service choose its own authentication
notes.back: B: Point clients at the single gateway address instead of the services.
notes.explanation: The secure-communication strategy says clients should not call target services directly but should point to the single gateway address.
notes.evidence: Clients should not be configured to call target services directly but rather to point to the single gateway URL.
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because it keeps the direct calls the strategy advises against. C is wrong because the guidance secures a microservices design rather than abandoning it. D is wrong because it scatters control instead of routing clients through one entry point.
notes.source: SP 800-204, §4.3 Strategies for Secure Communication Protocols (MS-SS-4)
